title: Investing in AI Literacy Means Investing in Judgment
summary: Knowing how to use an AI tool does not settle when to use it, what to trust it with, or
byline: Angel Chiang, Jewel Zhu, Paolo Miguel Ordonio

blocks.text: Knowing how to use an AI tool does not settle when to use it, what to trust it with, or how it can serve other people. These questions are part of AI literacy, alongside an understanding of the technology itself. Helping people make such judgments requires education that connects AI with their circumstances and responsibilities.

For Break the Fake Movement in the Philippines, this work builds on its focus on media and information literacy and countering disinformation. In a March 2026 research interview with the Centre for Asian Philanthropy and Society (CAPS), co-author Paolo Miguel Ordonio, Break the Fake Movement’s executive director, explained that its AI education emphasizes foundational understanding and critical thinking, and its curriculum includes ethics, copyright, data privacy and safety. He described enthusiasm for AI that does not always translate into understanding, alongside communities where some learners still need help with basic digital activities.

Different audiences also bring different needs. At the time of that interview, Break the Fake Movement was exploring how to adapt its AI literacy training for civil society workers through a collaboration with the Association of Foundations. Modules developed primarily for young people, parents and educators provided a starting point; understanding what civil society workers needed from AI education was part of the adaptation.

For civil society workers, AI literacy needs to address decisions they face at work: which problems AI can help solve, which tasks it can support, and where human judgment should remain central. CAPS’s report, Cars Without Roads: Investing in AI for Good Across Asia, illustrates the kinds of decisions people may face. Organizations approaching Infoxchange with plans to adopt AI sometimes discover that they first need better data management, stronger cybersecurity or a clearer definition of the problem they want to solve. In a separate CAPS interview, Hyomi Ahn, a researcher at Korea’s Beautiful Foundation, described its work to develop internal AI guidelines. She also highlighted debate among advocacy organizations about whether AI should draft public statements, raising questions about which work should remain human.

AI literacy programs can be designed for staff and leaders alike, with learning adapted to their different responsibilities. Staff may need to judge how AI fits their tasks; leaders may need to learn how to set expectations, develop guidance and provide time and resources for staff learning. The report’s findings on organizational readiness suggest that this education should also help people recognize when specialist advice is needed and what support colleagues need to apply their learning.

Yet funding for literacy education can be difficult to secure. Drawing on Break the Fake Movement’s experience, Ordonio described limited funding opportunities for literacy education, saying that funding favored infrastructure, tools and systems. His experience reflects the report’s wider concern that human capability and supporting conditions receive less investment than visible applications. In the study’s pre-interview survey of 36 organizations, 72.2% of respondents identified training and capacity-building as underinvested, the highest share for any category and more than double that of any other area.

blocks.text: For funders, this means supporting AI literacy programs that adapt learning to participants’ responsibilities and provide opportunities to consider where AI fits their work, whose needs it serves and what responsibilities its use entails. Funding this learning recognizes informed judgment as a capability worth developing and an essential part of turning technological possibilities into social value.
